papers.title: Classifying tumors from broad category to hierarchical molecular subtype: an interpretable hierarchical framework for precision oncology
papers.abstract: Precise tumor subtype classification is important for guiding personalized treatment, characterizing tumor heterogeneity, and investigating molecular mechanisms. However, most existing multi-label classification models use flat architectures and do not fully exploit the inherent hierarchical relationships and biological constraints among tumor types, which limits their performance and interpretability in complex, fine-grained pan-cancer classification. Here, we present the cancer Hallmark-based Hierarchical Recursive Model (HHRM) for pan-cancer hierarchical multi-label classification. HHRM integrates hierarchical label structures with recursive neural networks, enabling simultaneous modeling of multi-level dependencies from broad cancer categories to specific subtypes. We trained the model on a comprehensive pan-cancer cohort of 11,476 samples spanning 26 primary cancer types and 405 subtypes across up to eight hierarchical levels. HHRM achieved an accuracy of 0.7924 for predicting hierarchical tumor subtypes and was further evaluated on a validation dataset of 887 samples. Compared with other hierarchical modeling frameworks, HHRM achieved higher accuracy in all three output modes. Ablation experiments showed that replacing the hallmark-based graph convolutional network reduced model performance. On an independent dataset of 1,608 breast cancer samples, HHRM also achieved an accuracy greater than 0.86. Finally, we combined SHAP with a network-based method to rank and analyze predictive genes at different levels of the tumor hierarchy, which identified both known and potentially novel biomarkers for cancer diagnosis. In conclusion, to our knowledge, HHRM is the first hierarchical model for multi-level tumor subtype classification. Its competitive performance, combined with post hoc biological interpretation, suggests potential value for precision cancer diagnosis.

papers.title: TIGRdisco: a tool for the discovery of TIGR arrays and TIGR-associated Tas proteins from nucleotide sequences
papers.abstract: Tandem Interspaced Guide RNA (TIGR)-TIGR-associated protein (Tas) systems mediate DNA targeting through a hypercompact Tas effector, guided by dual spacers within a tigRNA that is processed from TIGR arrays. TIGR-Tas loci are composed of a Tas coding sequence associated with TIGR arrays of short units in either dual-repeat or stem-loop architecture. Unlike CRISPR (Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats) arrays that comprise units of direct repeats interspersed with unique spacers, units within the two distinct TIGR architectures only conform through extremely short box motifs, complicating detection. Here, we present TIGRdisco, an integrated tool capable of discovering both the Tas protein and its associated TIGR arrays directly from unannotated nucleotide sequences. TIGRdisco implements independent engines to detect the two array architectures through a motif-agnostic approach. We benchmarked TIGRdisco against a reference dataset of TIGR-Tas loci, recovering more than 80% of array units within its search window. Furthermore, TIGRdisco recovered arrays for loci within entire clades of Tas where associated arrays were unannotated in the reference. We found that these arrays largely contain non-canonical box motifs or unit lengths. Lastly, as a case study, we utilized TIGRdisco and successfully uncovered TIGR-Tas loci across metagenomic and genomic datasets.

papers.title: A protein language model for domain, functional site, and variant effect prediction
papers.abstract: Protein sequence databases are growing far faster than experimentally curated annotations, limiting functional interpretation of newly identified proteins and coding variants. We developed PALM, a protein annotation language model that jointly predicts domain and functional-site occurrence, while preserving overlapping and nested annotations through a soft-target objective. PALM integrates ESM2 with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), learned layer aggregation, and a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) encoder. PALM was trained on ~15 million InterPro-annotated UniRef50 sequences spanning 17,951 domain and 1,383 site classes. Across 2.3 million held-out proteins, PALM achieved domain- and site-occurrence F1 scores of 0.941 and 0.877, respectively, and retained substantial performance in proteins with <20% sequence identity to the training and validation data. PALM also substantially outperformed ESM3 annotation baseline. Without training on variant-pathogenicity labels, PALM embedding disruption distinguished 151,823 ClinVar missense variants more accurately than ESM2 embedding disruption (AUROC 0.835 versus 0.710), and combining PALM embedding disruption with the ESM2 likelihood-ratio signal reached an AUROC of 0.877. The same combined zero-shot score outperformed AlphaMissense on a benchmark dataset on 128,161 missense variants, that were derived from literature but not present in ClinVar database. At the protein level, PALM embeddings showed stronger CATH-Gene3D superfamily organization than frozen ESM2 and ESM3 embeddings, and improved prediction of experimental activation and repression effects when combined with ESM2. In a downstream case study, we demonstrated the ability to use PALM-derived embedding as proxy of deep mutational scanning (DMS), showcasing the broad application of PALM. Together, PALM converts curated residue-level knowledge into transferable and mechanistically interpretable representations that connect protein sequence, function, and variant consequence.

papers.title: Harnessing catalytic knowledge to guide enzyme discovery and evolution with AlphaEnzyme
papers.abstract: Retrieving an enzyme for a target reaction provides a starting point for evolution, but predicting how to improve it remains difficult. This requires connecting evolutionary information with the structural and chemical context of catalysis. Here we present AlphaEnzyme, an enzyme foundation model built on a structure-grounded representation of an enzyme paired with its reaction, from which catalytic compatibility, kinetics and mutational response are read out together. On a time-separated benchmark, AlphaEnzyme achieves a top-1 catalyst retrieval success rate of 30.1%, against 17.2% for the strongest baseline. Michaelis constant predictions achieve the highest rank correlations among the compared methods, reaching 0.64 for enzymes sharing at most 40% identity with the kinetic training set. The model also enriches high-fitness TrpB variants at a budget of 16 candidates without target-specific fitness training. In prospective transaminase engineering, several prioritized variants exceed the parent, with the best design yielding a 30.4-fold increase in product signal in a lysate-based assay while retaining (R)-selectivity. Together, AlphaEnzyme provides a common molecular basis for selecting starting enzymes and prioritizing sequence changes for their improvement.

papers.title: Earl Grey ParTEA: scalable, consistent transposable element annotation from pangenomes to deep phylogenetic scopes
papers.abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) are major drivers of genomic diversity, yet understanding their mobility and functional impact requires their accurate description in genomes. TE annotation is still typically performed genome-by-genome. TEs are often shared between some members of the same or closely related species. Hence, TE annotation with a library from a single reference misses families absent from that assembly, whereas building independent per-genome libraries fails to consistently surface shared TEs, hindering comparison. Here, we present Earl Grey ParTEA, a fully automated Snakemake pipeline extending the functionality of Earl Grey for comparative TE annotation across genome panels. ParTEA builds a single non-redundant TE library from all input genomes, resolves chimeric consensus sequences, and uses this shared library to annotate every genome, enabling direct comparison of TE family diversity, abundance, shared and private content, and activity landscapes. Optional modules provide TE library saturation analysis, BUSCO-based assembly quality control, and phylogenetic ordering of outputs. We applied ParTEA to sets of genomes spanning evolutionary scales: ten Arabidopsis thaliana accessions, ten Drosophila species, and ten species spanning the fungal kingdom. The Drosophila TE library expanded from 343 to 1,852 curated families including a previously missed rolling circle element with over 6,000 copies in D. miranda. The proportion of TE families shared across all genomes was highest within A. thaliana (97.3%), 37.7% across Drosophila species and only 0.5% across the set of fungi. ParTEA is available through Bioconda and represents a computationally efficient reproducible framework for comparative TE analysis in the era of large-scale genome analyses.

papers.title: FeatureMAP enables network-guided interpretation of untargeted metabolomics
papers.abstract: Untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) metabolomics generates thousands of features, but incomplete metabolite annotation and reliance on predefined pathways limit their biological interpretation. Here we present FeatureMAP, an LC-MS feature-centric computational framework that integrates multi-evidence metabolite annotation, network-guided refinement, metabolic module discovery, and structured large language model-based functional interpretation. Across ten public datasets, FeatureMAP improved MS1-based metabolite candidate prioritization while reducing annotation redundancy. In semi-synthetic benchmarks, FeatureMAP recovered coordinated metabolic perturbations, achieving 92% recovery of a simulated perturbation, and distinguished concurrent metabolic processes. Controlled benchmarks further evaluated functional interpretation under competing metabolite-level signals. Based on FeatureMAP, we additionally developed PhenoMAP, a phenotype-aware knowledge graph comprising 12,929 dysregulated metabolic modules from 501 human metabolomics studies spanning 326 phenotypes. Module-level comparisons revealed reproducible metabolic similarities across independent studies and biologically supported relationships among phenotypes. Application to Alzheimer's disease cerebrospinal fluid and cellular datasets identified convergent membrane-lipid alterations and implicated galactose-linked glycosphingolipid remodeling. Together, FeatureMAP and PhenoMAP enable network-grounded interpretation of incompletely annotated LC-MS metabolomics data and systematic investigation of metabolic dysregulation across biological conditions.

papers.title: MorphoProt: RNA-Conditioned Integration of Multiscale Histology for Spatial Protein Inference
papers.abstract: Spatially resolved protein abundance reveals cellular states and tissue organization that RNA expression cannot fully capture, yet direct spatial protein profiling remains costly and limited in coverage. Histology images routinely accompany spatial transcriptomics and offer complementary morphological information for protein inference. Here, we introduce MorphoProt, a multimodal framework that jointly predicts spatial protein abundance from RNA expression, multiscale histology and tissue neighborhoods. MorphoProt uses RNA-guided cross-attention over five histological fields of view, so that the morphological context read for each spot is conditioned on its molecular state. The fused representation is refined by gated aggregation of RNA-derived information from physical and transcriptomic neighborhoods before joint protein prediction. On held-out sections of human tonsil, mouse spleen and human liver, MorphoProt achieves mean proteinwise Spearman correlations of 0.652, 0.604 and 0.372, outperforming matched RNA-only and graph-based baselines and the histology-based HIPI and multimodal SPRINT baselines in all three tissues. Combining fields of view, rather than any single one, carries the histology gain: in spleen and liver, the multiscale model outperforms every single-field model, and its learned scale preference separates white-pulp from red-pulp compartments. Predicted proteins preserve protein-defined tissue domains and their marker identity, and recover pathologist-annotated germinal centers as accurately as measured proteins.

papers.title: Reconstruction of Cellular Trajectories with Biologically Interpretable States
papers.abstract: Elucidating the trajectories of cellular evolution provides biologists with deeper insights into biological systems and disease progression, ultimately facilitating more informed discovery of mechanisms and therapeutic design. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is widely used to study cellular evolution. However, it faces two primary limitations. First, because the process destroys cells during gene-expression measurement, it is impossible to track the gene-expression profile of the same cell throughout the entire trajectory. Second, because scRNA-seq captures cells at discrete time points, it provides only static snapshots rather than continuous trajectories, limiting its ability to resolve the full dynamics of cellular transitions. Consequently, various computational approaches have been developed to address these challenges. However, existing models fail to capture the hidden state of each cell, which is essential for reconstructing gene expression at unobserved time points. As the gene expression profiles depend on the cell state, and may vary according to time, we propose a Latent Cell-State Model, where we approximate cell state transition as a Markov chain and obtain the gene expression of each cell at unobserved timepoints depending on the cell state, time, and a latent variable that represents the high-dimensional gene expression profile of a cell. Our model is able to infer biologically meaningful cell states and generate high-quality gene expression profiles at unobserved timepoints, showing potential for accurate trajectory reconstruction.

papers.title: Quantitative Spatial Analysis of Matrix Remodelling in Wounds Using Digital Pathology and Fractal Analysis
papers.abstract: Wound healing involves spatially heterogeneous changes in matrix composition and organisation that can be difficult to capture using qualitative histological assessment alone. We developed a reproducible digital pathology workflow to quantify matrix features in cutaneous wound sections, compare them with unwounded skin, and derive an exploratory Histological Wound Index (HWI). Four normal-skin and six wound sections were analysed using QuPath, ImageJ/FracLac and Python. Approximately 500 x 500 micrometer regions of interest (ROI) were assigned to normal skin, wound centre, proximal edge or distant edge. Collagen, mucin and necrotic tissue coverage were quantified using image classifiers and analysed with linear mixed-effects models. Collagen architecture was assessed from collagen-selective binary masks using fractal dimension and lacunarity. Collagen coverage, fractal dimension, mucin coverage, necrosis and lacunarity were z-standardised and integrated into the HWI. Unwounded skin showed high collagen coverage and fractal dimension, with low lacunarity, mucin and necrosis. In contrast, wound-centre tissue showed low collagen coverage and fractal dimension together with higher mucin and necrosis. Distant-edge regions retained comparatively normal-like characteristics, whereas proximal-edge regions showed intermediate values. HWI was highest in normal skin and lowest in the wound centre. A descriptive matched-ROI comparison of two wound sections reproduced this regional ordering when all component measures were derived from identical ROI boundaries. This workflow provides a reproducible framework for quantifying regional ECM features and collagen-mask architecture in wound histology. The HWI is an exploratory histological summary requiring validation in larger longitudinal datasets.

papers.title: memVar: an integrated resource for interpreting human membrane protein variation in molecular and disease contexts
papers.abstract: Interpreting membrane protein variation requires connecting clinical evidence to the membrane environments and molecular interactions that govern protein functions. Here, we introduce memVar (https://memvar.sunnylab.org), an integrated database of 10,906,688unique single-nucleotide variants from ClinVar, COSMIC, and gnomAD across 7,732 human membrane-associated proteins. memVar reconciles genomic, transcript, and protein coordinates to link variants with membrane topology, bilayer depth, lipid contacts, functional sites, partner-specific interaction interfaces, and variant-effect predictions, alongside disease, tissue-expression and regulatory annotations. Coordinated sequence, structure and variant views retain source provenance and distinguish clinical assertions, experimental observations, and computational predictions. Our analysis reveals that pathogenic/likely pathogenic missense substitutions are enriched in transmembrane segments and predicted protein-protein interaction sites relative to benign/likely benign substitutions, with pooled odds ratios of 2.47 and 6.67, respectively. IntAct-derived interaction loss or decrease was experimentally recorded for 57.9% of pathogenic/likely pathogenic substitutions versus 7.4% of benign/likely benign substitutions. CFTR examples contextualize the established G551D gating defect and prioritize W202R, a variant of uncertain significance, for tests of protein maturation, surface abundance and channel activity. By connecting variant records to specific molecular questions, memVar potentially supports mechanism-oriented investigation and prioritization of functional experiments.

papers.title: Improving phosphoproteomic kinase activity inference by contextual refinement of Kinase Library relationships
papers.abstract: Kinase activity inference from phosphoproteomic data relies on kinase-specific substrate sets defined by kinase-substrate relationship (KSR) priors. Kinase Library (KL) expands candidate substrate coverage using experimentally derived kinase specificity profiles, but its predictions reflect sequence compatibility rather than established intracellular regulation. We benchmarked KL-expanded KSR priors using 222 perturbation phosphoproteomic samples covering 396 annotated activation or inhibition events across 78 kinases. Broad KL expansion increased the number of scoreable kinases from 108 to 391, but reduced perturbed-kinase discrimination, directional accuracy and ranking performance. Higher error rates occurred among kinases with limited curated substrate support, while broad expansion also increased redundancy among inferred activity profiles. To improve the reliability of motif-derived relationships, we constrained KL-derived KSRs using predicted protein co-localization and protein-association evidence. Protein-association filtering consistently improved inference performance, reduced activity redundancy and provided a more favorable accuracy-coverage balance than co-localization filtering. The selected protein-association-filtered prior retained activity estimates for 308 kinases with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) above 0.75 and extended inference to 200 kinases not scoreable using curated KSRs, which were significantly enriched for dark kinases. These newly scoreable kinases showed structured activity patterns across perturbation contexts and interpretable signaling associations. Our results show that protein-association evidence can refine motif-derived KSR priors while preserving broad kinome coverage, providing a practical framework for more reliable phosphoproteomic kinase activity inference.

papers.title: A comparative transcriptomic framework across kidney organoid, assembloid, and transplantation models
papers.abstract: Human kidney organoids recapitulate key aspects of renal development and have emerged as valuable platforms for disease modeling, nephrotoxicity screening, and therapeutic development. The field now includes a wide range of emerging protocols with distinct cellular compositions and maturation states, which complicates systematic comparison and model selection. Here, we integrated single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomes from 11 studies spanning kidney organoid and assembloids, both in vitro and following transplantation, benchmarked against fetal and adult kidney references. Transcriptional maturation toward adult identity is compartment specific and does not correlate with protocol complexity. Assembloid protocols show the most adult-like podocyte and distal nephron signatures, transplantation is associated with enhanced tubular oxidative metabolic features, only protocols incorporating ureteric progenitors reliably generate collecting-duct lineages, and no protocol achieves mature adult proximal tubule identity. Annotating against either fetal or adult kidney reference alone leads to misassignment, because early fetal nephron epithelium transcriptionally resembles injury-dedifferentiated adult proximal tubule cells. Assembloid and transplantation models share elevated mechanosensing pathway expression independently of vascularization. Together, these findings provide a framework for kidney organoid model selection.

papers.title: Benchmarking Statistical Methods for Differential Composition Analysis in Population-Scale Single-Cell Data
papers.abstract: Population-scale single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data capture cellular composition across cohorts ranging from several dozen to thousands of individuals, enabling the detection of cell-type composition differences between conditions. These differences reveal cellular shifts in disease pathogenesis and suggest potential targets for therapeutic intervention. However, differential composition analysis in scRNA-seq data is challenged by the unique features of cell count data, such as compositionality, prevalence of zeros, overdispersion, and confounding by technical and biological covariates. While this analysis is routinely performed, no study has yet systematically evaluated existing methods. Here, we benchmarked 12 methods for differential composition analysis using three population-scale scRNA-seq datasets with diverse and representative characteristics. Analyses of real data revealed low agreement across methods, while permutations and simulations based on the real data demonstrated excessive false discoveries for most methods. Overall, LOCOM emerged as the top-performing method that controls the false discovery rate while maintaining good statistical power, followed by ANCOM-BC and linear regression with centered-log-ratio transformation. Integrating evidence from real-data analyses and data-informed permutation and simulation experiments, we provide practical guidance tailored to common real-world challenges in differential composition analysis.

papers.title: RPI-Zero: Zero-shot RNA-Protein Interaction Prediction
papers.abstract: In vivo protein-RNA interactions are mapped almost exclusively by CLIP-seq, which profiles one protein in one cell type per experiment and needs a specific antibody; only about 10% of the roughly 2,000 human RNA-binding proteins have been assayed, and the Protein Data Bank holds around 5,000 protein-RNA complexes, a quarter of them ribosomes. Sequence-based prediction could extend coverage to unprofiled, newly discovered, or designed molecules, but existing predictors are not built for that case. One family trains a separate model per protein and cannot move beyond proteins with CLIP data; the other scores pairs but targets a single RNA class. Most are evaluated with random splits and randomly paired negatives that leave near-identical sequences on both sides of the split, and many require structure or read only short windows, discarding the context around a binding site. Their accuracy falls sharply when whole molecules are held out. We address this with two contributions. First, a strict benchmark of 2.1 million examples built from 11.6 million peaks of CLIP experiments targeting 209 proteins, taken from four public databases, in which each RNA is a spliced transcript with nucleotide-level labels, and sequence-similarity clusters are assigned whole to training, validation, and test sets, giving separate slices for unseen RNAs, unseen proteins, and unseen pairs. Negatives are matched to positives in length and in the number of other proteins binding the transcript, removing the shortcut by which a model predicts binding from how popular a transcript is without reading the protein. Second, RPI-Zero, a sequence-only model that reads any full-length protein and RNA jointly in up to 4,096 tokens, so the RNA representation is conditioned on the protein, and describes every protein as a mixture of shared motif prototypes, placing unseen proteins in the same terms as training ones. One model covers all proteins and RNA classes, uses no structure, and needs no interaction data for a new molecule. Compared with five state-of-the-art methods, it achieves the highest score in eight different metrics on unseen RNAs, unseen proteins, and unseen pairs. The model and data are available at https://github.com/ciceklab/RPI-Zero and https://zenodo.org/records/23748141, respectively.

papers.title: FoldAbS: Repurposing the Protein Folding Model as a Foundation Encoder for Antibody Screening
papers.abstract: Therapeutic antibody screening requires prioritizing antibody candidates across specificity, affinity, and developability. Current pipelines typically silo these objectives and underuse structural information that governs antibody-antigen recognition. To address these inefficacies, we introduce FoldAbS, a unified supervised screening framework that reconceptualizes protein folding models as frozen foundation encoders, exploiting their internal representations to capture rich sequence, geometric, and interaction dynamics well beyond basic structure prediction. By coupling the folding model with lightweight, task-specific heads, FoldAbS seamlessly evaluates all three therapeutic criteria within a single architecture. Instantiating this framework with the open-source Protenix model (FoldAbS-Px) yields consistent improvements over baseline approaches, achieving significant performance gains of up to 13.1%, 9.2%, and 6.2% in specificity, affinity, and developability, respectively. Collectively, these results reposition protein folding models from structure predictors and confidence scorers into reusable foundation encoders for comprehensive and supervised antibody screening. Our code is available at https://github.com/nohandsomewujun/FoldAbS.

papers.title: PartiDesign: A structure-sequence co-design paradigm for practical all-to-all biomolecules design
papers.abstract: Engineering interactions among biomolecules offers a route to creating new biological functions. Although unified models have advanced biomolecular structure prediction and design, efficient and controllable generation across molecular modalities remains challenging. A key challenge is to couple three-dimensional structure generation with sequence or chemical-identity design across chemically diverse systems. Here, we introduce PartiDesign, a unified structure-sequence co-design model that extends the partially latent framework of La-Proteina to proteins, nucleic acids and small molecules. PartiDesign jointly generates molecular structures and their corresponding sequences or chemical identities, while providing fine-grained control over secondary structure, chemical bonding and amino acid preferences. Across diverse benchmarks for the de novo design of proteins, nucleic acids and small molecules against specified targets, PartiDesign achieved the highest estimated successful-design throughput among the evaluated methods on most benchmarks under the adopted compute-budget protocols. Its configurable constraints further support cyclic peptide and antibody design, allowing generation to be tailored to specific structural and chemical requirements. PartiDesign was developed using 128 Huawei Ascend 910B accelerators, each with 64 GB of memory. The source code is available at https://github.com/MegaGatlingPea/PartiDesign-official, and a freely accessible web server at https://cadd.zju.edu.cn/partidesign/ enables users to generate binding partners without programming expertise. Together, these capabilities provide a versatile and accessible framework for all-to-all biomolecular design, with applications in molecular engineering and drug discovery.

papers.title: OncoSpot enables benchmarking of cancer spatial transcriptomics methods across tumor evolutionary modes
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) is increasingly used to map clonal architecture within tumors, yet methods for analyzing cancer ST data are difficult to evaluate because real tumors lack ground truth for copy-number alterations (CNAs), subclonal identity, and malignant cell fraction. Existing ST simulators model normal tissue and do not represent tumor evolution, CNA-driven expression, or the spatial organization of malignant subclones. We present OncoSpot, a cancer-aware simulator of Visium-like spot-based ST data. OncoSpot combines a spatial evolutionary scaffold from DEMON, CNAs generated along the resulting clonal phylogeny with CNAsim, cancer-type-specific malignant transcriptional programs, and spatially clustered nonmalignant cell types, and aggregates cells into spots with known malignant fraction, subclone, and copy-number profiles. We demonstrate OncoSpot on high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, colorectal cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma, which represent three distinct modes of tumor evolution. Simulated subclones were spatially clustered and showed stronger phylogeny-space concordance than those generated by scCube under matched subclone populations. Benchmarking CopyKAT, CancerFinder, Clonalscope, and RCTD revealed cancer-dependent performance: Clonalscope recovered copy-number signals more accurately in ovarian and colorectal cancer, whereas CopyKAT performed better in hepatocellular carcinoma, reflecting both the assumptions of each method and the copy-number landscapes of the three cancers. OncoSpot's ground truth also exposed a failure mode in Clonalscope's malignant spot identification, in which tumor and normal labels were inverted, and allowed us to trace its cause. These method-dependent behaviors would be difficult to detect in real data. OncoSpot provides a framework for benchmarking CNA inference, subclone detection, malignant spot identification, and normal spot deconvolution, and its modular design and guidelines allow extension to additional cancer types. OncoSpot is freely available at https://github.com/compbio-mallory/OncoSpot.

papers.title: TRACE: a framework for traceable biomedical resource construction demonstrated through single-cell glaucoma data
papers.abstract: The growing availability of public omics datasets presents opportunities for biomedical research, yet constructing research question-driven resources from distributed studies remains challenging due to heterogeneous data, incomplete metadata and limited documentation of curation decisions. Here, we present TRACE (Traceable Resource Assembly and Curation Ecosystem), a general framework that links systematic knowledge discovery, data curation and resource delivery while preserving provenance throughout resource construction. We demonstrate TRACE through TRACE-scGlaucoma, a curated single-cell transcriptomics resource for glaucoma and optic nerve biology. Systematic screening identified 57 eligible studies, of which 42 provided accessible datasets comprising approximately 3.3 million cells. The resource provides harmonised metadata, standardised cell-type annotations and reusable expression objects while retaining original study information and curation provenance. We demonstrate its analytical utility through cellular enrichment of glaucoma GWAS-associated genes, comparing candidate drug-repurposing signals across distinct biological contexts and assessment of cell-type annotation reliability. TRACE provides a systematic and traceable approach to transforming fragmented public datasets into reusable biomedical resources, supporting reproducible analyses and future extensions across disease areas and data modalities.

papers.title: Multi-objective domain adaptation for pan-cancer transfer of pharmacogenomic drug response to patient tumours
papers.abstract: Large-scale pharmacogenomic screens provide rich drug-sensitivity measurements in cancer cell lines, but transferring these measurements to patient tumours remains limited by biological heterogeneity and cross-domain distribution shift. Existing machine learning approaches, including adversarial autoencoder and domain adaptation, address this gap by learning shared latent representations between preclinical models and patient samples. However, alignment without explicit biological constraints can produce unreliable representations when cancer lineage structure and clinically relevant patient heterogeneity are not preserved. Here, we introduce MODAE+, a pan-cancer multi-objective deep learning domain adaptation framework that jointly balances domain alignment, deconfounding, drug-response prediction, survival prediction, and cancer-lineage classification across 9,696 TCGA tumours, 1,293 CCLE cancer cell lines, and CTRP sensitivity profiles for 544 compounds in 738 matched cell lines. This multi-objective design improved cross-domain alignment while preserving cancer-lineage organization and patient heterogeneity. For drugs shared between the pharmacogenomic screen and TCGA treatment records, MODAE+ predicted sensitivity was significantly associated with overall survival among patients who received each drug in 46.3% of evaluated cancer-drug pairs by log-rank testing and 41.5% by multivariable Cox analysis. Biological validation across four curated drug-gene resources identified significant expression differences exceeding 1.5-fold for 34.9-64.4% of drugs in pan-cancer analyses, based on the lowest-p-value annotated gene per drug. Drug-class-specific patterns involved intended molecular targets for targeted therapies and predominantly transport, metabolism, detoxification and resistance-related genes for classical chemotherapies. As an additional validation, we derived pretreatment responder-nonresponder gene-expression signatures from 13 external breast cancer datasets and evaluated their concordance with MODAE+ predictions across 69 signature-drug comparisons in TCGA patients treated with paclitaxel or doxorubicin. Consensus signature scores showed Spearman correlations of 0.791 with predicted paclitaxel sensitivity and 0.724 with predicted doxorubicin sensitivity, averaging 0.758 across the two drugs. Together, these complementary analyses provide supporting evidence for the clinical relevance and biological consistency of MODAE+ predictions, suggesting their potential to identify drug-sensitive tumour subgroups and generate hypotheses about mechanisms of drug resistance.

papers.title: Clinical-Anchored Incremental Survival Learning: A Stability-Constrained Framework for Molecularly Enhanced Survival Prediction in Lung Adenocarcinoma
papers.abstract: Accurate survival prediction in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) remains challenging because high-dimensional molecular data can introduce overfitting and unstable feature selection. We developed Clinical-Anchored Incremental Survival Learning (CAISL), a framework that integrates a sparse molecular risk correction with a clinical baseline to improve prognostic discrimination while constraining model complexity and prediction variability. CAISL was evaluated using The Cancer Genome Atlas LUAD cohort comprising 470 patients and 119 observed deaths. Performance was compared with clinical Cox, molecular-only, and unanchored multimodal models using five independently seeded, event-stratified five-fold cross-validation runs. CAISL achieved a mean concordance index (C-index) of 0.7246, compared with 0.6970 for clinical Cox, yielding an absolute improvement of 0.0276 (95% bootstrap confidence interval [CI], 0.005 to 0.050). Time-dependent discrimination was higher at three years (AUC, 0.742 vs. 0.712) and five years (AUC, 0.721 vs. 0.691), while the integrated Brier score was lower for CAISL than for clinical Cox (0.164 vs. 0.181). Ablation analysis identified clinical anchoring as the component associated with the largest reduction in discrimination when removed. Stability analysis showed a mean pairwise Jaccard similarity of 0.46 between selected feature sets and a mean Spearman correlation of 0.86 between molecular correction scores. These findings support the potential of clinically anchored, stability-constrained molecular learning to improve internal survival-risk prediction in LUAD. Independent-cohort validation is needed to establish generalizability.

papers.title: Cross-cancer knowledge transfer for lymph node metastasis prediction: Applicability of an axillary lymph node-based deep learning model
papers.abstract: Evaluation of lymph node (LN) metastasis is critical for cancer staging and treatment planning. Since radiologic hallmarks of metastatic LNs are shared across primary cancers, a computed tomography (CT)-based deep learning (DL) classifier developed from one anatomy may transfer to others. This study built a DenseNet-121 ensemble model using clinical-implication-applied preprocessing and evaluated its cross-anatomical generalizability to LNs from diverse primary cancers. A DenseNet-121 ensemble model combining fixed-size cropping (FSC) and adjustable square cropping (ASC) was trained from ImageNet initialization on an axillary lymph node (ALN) dataset (n = 1,128 from 523 breast cancer patients). The model utilized clinical-implication-applied perinodal cropping with bicubic filtering and standardized resizing. To test cross-anatomical generalizability, an external dataset of 256 CT images across four anatomical regions was evaluated: cervical, mediastinal, upper-abdominal, and lower-abdominal LNs. Perinodal free margins were systematically varied from 10% to 40% to optimize the balance between context preservation and surround interference. Bicubic filtering and standardized resizing yielded the highest internal performance on the original ALN dataset (FSC-ASC ensemble area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.958, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.920-0.987 at 40% margin). The model demonstrated site-dependent, above-chance generalizability across all external regions. Cervical LNs achieved the highest performance at a 40% margin (AUROC 0.939, 95% CI 0.875-0.989). Mediastinal LNs peaked at a 10% margin (AUROC 0.796, 95% CI 0.672-0.903), with wider margins degrading performance due to adjacent structural interference. Upper-abdominal and lower-abdominal LNs reached optimal performance at a 30% margin (AUROC 0.814 for upper; AUROC 0.917 for lower). A single ALN-trained DL model can accurately predict LN metastasis across cervical, mediastinal, and abdominal stations through site-specific perinodal margin tuning. These findings support the feasibility of cross-cancer knowledge transfer and the clinical utility of generalizable backbones for pan-cancer nodal assessment.

papers.title: CARTnet: Template-guided B-cell Epitope Prediction with Contact-aware Attention
papers.abstract: B-cell epitope prediction remains challenging due to the limited availability of experimentally characterized data and the incomplete understanding of antibody-antigen recognition. Here, we present CARTnet, a novel contact-aware deep learning framework that integrates multimodal features and template-derived epitope information. CARTnet demonstrated superior performance when compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods across most evaluation metrics on both the internal and external test datasets. In particular, CARTnet achieved an AUPRC of 0.243 on the internal test set, compared with 0.220 for DiscoTope-3, 0.140 for BepiPred-2, and 0.198 for BepiPred-3. This improvement was also observed on the external test set, where CARTnet achieved an AUPRC of 0.267, compared with 0.192, 0.111, and 0.215 for DiscoTope-3, BepiPred-2, and BepiPred-3, respectively, supporting its generalizability. CARTnet also supports template-guided prediction, in which limited prior epitope information can improve the identification of additional epitope residues; a single template residue increased the AUPRC of the template-based variant from 0.225 to 0.403 on the internal test set. Furthermore, we demonstrated that epitope information from closely related viruses can be transferred across the genus Alphavirus to improve epitope prediction accuracy. These results establish CARTnet as an accurate framework for both de novo and template-guided B-cell epitope prediction.

papers.title: Autonomous generalizability auditing of scientific foundation models
papers.abstract: Determining where scientific foundation models generalize beyond their development data is essential for reliable use, but aggregate benchmarks obscure performance limits and rigorous audits are difficult to conduct routinely. Here, we introduce AutoSPECTRA, a coding-agent protocol for systematic generalizability auditing. To inform its design, we reviewed 38 studies across five biological domains and evaluated coding agents, which generated hypotheses and empirical analyses but applied inconsistent standards for judging evidence. We then structured AutoSPECTRA around measurable generalization axes, prespecified analyses, controlled comparisons and independent confirmation. Across four biological foundation models, audits linked performance to protein sequence composition and relatedness to pretraining data (ESMFold2), representation of perturbations in training (STATE), effective spatial resolution (CONCH), and residue-level genomic, evolutionary and structural context (AlphaMissense). Agents also evaluated alternative explanations and rejected unsupported hypotheses. AutoSPECTRA provides a systematic approach to discovering and testing the limits of scientific foundation models.

papers.title: brisc: a multithreaded CPU toolkit for single-cell analysis
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing datasets have grown from tens of thousands of cells to tens of millions. At this scale, standard toolkits like Scanpy and Seurat need hours per analysis, hindering iterative exploration. We present brisc, the first end-to-end multithreaded CPU toolkit for single-cell analysis, spanning dimensionality reduction, integration, label transfer, clustering, embedding, differential expression and plotting. Unlike GPU-based counterparts, brisc strictly guarantees reproducibility: identical results between runs, regardless of thread count. Algorithmic innovations include a blocked inverted-file-index-based nearest-neighbors algorithm that makes 81-98% fewer errors than Scanpy and Seurat. On a 192-CPU node, brisc ran a standard workflow on 10 million cells in 3 minutes, 116x faster than Scanpy at under half its peak memory usage and 236x faster than Seurat with BPCells. On 96 CPUs, it matched the speed of rapids-singlecell on four H100 GPUs. brisc enables near-real-time, reproducible analysis of tens of millions of cells without specialized hardware.

papers.title: HiFiTaxa: a reproducible analysis pipeline for full length 16S rRNA gene and ITS amplicon sequencing from PacBio reads
papers.abstract: Long-read amplicon sequencing profiles communities at high resolution, but taxonomic accuracy depends on the reference, classifier and the parameters used. Here, we present HiFiTaxa, a reproducible, single command Nextflow pipeline for PacBio HiFi 16S rRNA gene and fungal ITS amplicons. It builds versioned references from current GTDB and UNITE releases and supports Bayesian lowest common ancestor (BLCA) and naive Bayes (NB) classifiers and the read level profilers Emu (16S rRNA gene) and EMITS (ITS). We benchmarked them on mock communities and on holdouts with 10% of GTDB or UNITE databases sequences withheld. On the 16S rRNA gene mock of 20 species, BLCA detected all 20 species and reported two false positives, NB detected 17 and reported none, and Emu detected all 20 and reported eight. In the GTDB holdout, for taxa represented in the reference, BLCA reached 80.0% species level accuracy against 48.1% for the exact matching species step of NB. However, NB produced fewer incorrect assignments for taxa absent from the reference. On fungal ITS, BLCA had slightly higher holdout accuracy at species level(54.7%) against 52.2% for NB. NB was more conservative for novel taxa, and EMITS detected the most mock species. HiFiTaxa therefore offers a single reproducible workflow that uses current GTDB and UNITE releases and enables users to choose between different classifier algorithms depending on their needs.

papers.title: Error-Controlled Discovery of Protein Interactions via Conformal Calibration
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are powerful predictors of protein interactions, but strong benchmark performance does not ensure reliable discoveries. We introduce PPI-Caliper, a model-agnostic framework that adapts conformal calibration to select interactions at user-specified false discovery rate (FDR) levels using held-out labels without retraining the predictor. Across five species, two PLM-based predictors, and two human training-data versions for each predictor, PPI-Caliper keeps empirical FDR at or below the target level under in-distribution calibration. Under distribution shift, transferred thresholds tend to become conservative when predictive performance improves, but can fail to control FDR when performance deteriorates. PPI-Caliper connects pre-trained interaction scores to explicit error targets and demonstrates why reliable biological discovery requires evaluating calibration alongside predictive accuracy.

papers.title: Where single-cell foundation models help: a benchmark of annotation, perturbation and regulatory inference against simple baselines
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models (FMs) are proposed as general tools for cell-type annotation, in silico perturbation and gene-regulatory-network (GRN) inference. To identify where they add value, we benchmarked five FMs (scGPT, Geneformer V1 and V2, Nicheformer, scFoundation), CellOracle, supervised perturbation models including STATE, and task-matched simple baselines on the same data, from K562 Perturb-seq screens and primary cells to healthy-donor and isogenic leukodystrophy brain organoids, a public organoid CRISPR screen and lung cancer biopsies. FMs were most useful when labels had to be transferred across species: from human to mouse lung, Nicheformer reached 0.98 accuracy and Geneformer V2 and scFoundation about 0.90, against 0.68 for the best baseline. Zero-shot in silico perturbations captured the direction of real responses in K562, with up to 75% of perturbations shifted in the expected direction (scFoundation, p < 1e-8), and Geneformer V2 networks recovered patient-level tumour differential expression better than co-expression (fold enrichment 2.9 versus 2.0). Within a species, FM embeddings annotated cells as accurately as principal components. In organoids, predicted knockout effects were largely explained by where the target is expressed, and an expression-matched control test isolated the gene-specific part, 12 to 35% of the effects. Isogenic Canavan and Krabbe organoids and 4H patient organoids, with one library per line and time point, did not yet separate methods from differences between clones and donors, which defines the replication needed for future validation. Fine-tuning changed classification accuracy but not knockout rankings. We release the benchmark, baselines, pipeline checks and the isogenic reference task as the fmaudit package, so that new models can be evaluated on the tasks where FMs already help.

papers.title: Representation-aware calibration enables statistically reliable protein structure search
papers.abstract: Searching large databases of predicted protein structures can reveal remote homologs, but reliable discovery requires accurate significance estimates. We show that native E-values reported by protein structure search tools such as Foldseek and Reseek can be unreliable, leading to false discoveries or missed homologs. To address this problem, we introduce Struct-Caliper, which provides reliable query-specific p-values for protein structure search. The method uses representation-aware query randomization to generate background queries and compares observed alignment scores with the highest scores from randomized searches of the same database. In simulations, SG p-values generally kept reported false positive at or below the chosen cutoff under the evaluated randomization procedures. In searches of 15,177 ASTRAL40 structures, SG p-values increased Foldseek homolog recovery by 18.2% with slightly fewer false discoveries compared with native E-values at a cutoff of 0.01. For Reseek, false discoveries even decreased by 99.5%. Across 73 queries searched against more than two million AlphaFoldDB structures, SG p-values increased the mean recovery of DALI-supported matches by 23.5% at the same cutoff. These results show that Struct-Caliper can improve the reliability of structure searches and help prioritize discoveries for further biological analysis.

papers.title: Evaluating the Identifiability of Temporal Delay and Response Attenuation in Endometrial Decidualization
papers.abstract: Endometriosis is associated with impaired endometrial decidualization, yet conventional differential expres-sion analyses cannot readily distinguish delayed transcriptional activation from reduced response amplitude.These mechanisms may produce similar expression differences at individual time points while implying distinct biological interpretations. Establishing when they can be distinguished is therefore a computational identifiability problem.We implement an identifiability-aware analysis of temporal displacement and amplitude attenuation in longitudinal transcriptomic responses. The approach combines reference trajectories, constrained amplitude-only and amplitude-plus-delay models, analytical examples of observational equivalence, and simulation-based assessments of mechanism distinguishability. Held-out time-point evaluation and culture-level sensitivity analyses examine the stability of model-dependent conclusions.In GSE246591, a candidate-delay-dependent dynamic-range filter excluded 30.9 - 38.3% of initially dynamic features under a hypothetical 24-hour shift across four endometrial stromal cultures. A two-component diagnostic separating retained dynamic range from affine shape similarity revealed that small projection residuals can arise from either loss of observable dynamics or similarity of response shapes. These findings demonstrate why a single separation statistic may be insufficient for interpreting temporal identifiability.Complementary independent in vivo analyses provided biological context. In GSE51981, an endometrial progesterone-response-associated transcriptional score was reduced in endometriosis samples (phase-model estimate 0.155, 95% CI 0.222 to 0.088). GSE6364 showed a directionally consistent but statistically inconclusive difference (0.033, 95% CI 0.068 to 0.002). Neither observation independently establishes a temporal delay.Together, these results support selection-aware evaluation of temporal transcriptomic responses, distin-guishing structural ambiguity and loss of dynamic signal from evidence of a biological timing change.

papers.title: Missing by design: why genomic metadata must be captured at submission, not recovered from the literature
papers.abstract: Plant and metazoan genome assemblies are being deposited in the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC) archives at an accelerating rate, but the biological context needed to interpret them, such as ploidy, cultivar, and subgenome structure, is often missing from the record: these attributes are optional in most submission checklists and, when supplied, are entered as free text. We describe the gap in three layers. Ploidy varies within a species and cannot be inferred from taxonomy; chromosome-naming conventions differ between assemblies of the same crop; and that inconsistency is concentrated in species named by subgenome and is not associated with the size of the research community, which points to the lack of a shared convention. As a case study, we built a pipeline that recovers these attributes from the publications linked to an assembly. On a benchmark of 82 assemblies, its current version reported one wrong ploidy, and across 1,059 plant assemblies an earlier, less strict version found the ploidy in a publication for about half; for nearly a third, it found a publication but no statement of ploidy in it. Recovery from the literature can annotate assemblies already deposited but cannot stop new ones from arriving incomplete. We therefore propose that ploidy, cultivar, and subgenome structure be captured at submission as mandatory, controlled-vocabulary attributes, building on existing INSDC and Genomic Standards Consortium checklists.
